claim: In 64-bit mode x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers and a default operand size of 32 bits.
quote: In 64-bit mode, there are 16 general purpose registers and the default operand size is 32 bits.

claim: The 64-bit general-purpose register names are RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RSP, RBP and R8 through R15.
quote: 64-bit general-purpose registers (RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RSP, RBP, or R8-R15).

claim: The 32-bit forms are named EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX, ESI, EDI, ESP, EBP and R8D-R15D, the 16-bit forms AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI, SP, BP and R8W-R15W, and the 8-bit forms AL, BL, CL, DL, SIL, DIL, SPL, BPL and R8B-R15B, the last group requiring a REX prefix.
quote: 32-bit general-purpose registers (EAX, EBX, ECX, EDX, ESI, EDI, ESP, EBP, or R8D-R15D). 16-bit general-purpose registers (AX, BX, CX, DX, SI, DI, SP, BP, or R8W-R15W). 8-bit general-purpose registers: AL, BL, CL, DL, SIL, DIL, SPL, BPL, and R8B-R15B are available using REX prefixes

claim: A write to the 32-bit form of a register produces a 32-bit result that is zero-extended to fill the whole 64-bit register.
quote: 32-bit operands generate a 32-bit result, zero-extended to a 64-bit result in the destination general-purpose register.

claim: Unlike 32-bit writes, 8-bit and 16-bit operands leave the upper 56 or 48 bits of the destination register unchanged.
quote: 8-bit and 16-bit operands generate an 8-bit or 16-bit result. The upper 56 bits or 48 bits (respectively) of the destination general-purpose register are not modified by the operation.

claim: x86-64 is little-endian: the bytes of a word are numbered starting from the least significant byte.
quote: Intel 64 and IA-32 processors are “little endian” machines; this means the bytes of a word are numbered starting from the least significant byte.

claim: CMP sets the CF, OF, SF, ZF, AF and PF status flags according to the result, the same flags it sets in the same manner as SUB.
quote: The CF, OF, SF, ZF, AF, and PF flags are set according to the result.

claim: The signed conditional jump JLE (JNG) is taken when ZF is 1 or the exclusive-or of SF and OF is 1.
quote: JLE/JNG ((SF xor OF) or ZF) = 1 Less or equal/not greater

claim: On a near call the processor pushes the return address (the address of the instruction following the CALL) on the stack and then branches to the target.
quote: When executing a near call, the processor pushes the value of the EIP register (which contains the offset of the instruction following the CALL instruction) on the stack (for use later as a return-instruction pointer). The processor then branches to the address in the current code segment specified by the target operand.

claim: On a near return the processor pops the return instruction pointer from the top of the stack into the instruction pointer register and resumes execution there.
quote: When executing a near return, the processor pops the return instruction pointer (offset) from the top of the stack into the EIP register and begins program execution at the new instruction pointer. The CS register is unchanged.

claim: LEA computes the effective address of its source operand and stores that address in the destination register.
quote: Computes the effective address of the second operand (the source operand) and stores it in the first operand (destination operand).

claim: LEA affects no flags.
quote: None.

claim: An x86 memory operand is base + index*scale + disp with scale one of 1, 2, 4 or 8, written in AT&T syntax as disp(base, index, scale).
quote:
An Intel syntax indirect memory reference of the form
section:[base + index*scale + disp]
is translated into the AT&T syntax
section:disp(base, index, scale)

claim: x86-64 adds instruction-pointer-relative addressing, written with rip as the base register, and only constant offsets are valid.
quote: The x86-64 architecture adds an RIP (instruction pointer relative) addressing. This addressing mode is specified by using ‘rip’ as a base register. Only constant offsets are valid.

claim: LEAVE copies the frame pointer into the stack pointer, releasing the frame, then pops the saved old frame pointer back into the frame-pointer register.
quote: The LEAVE instruction copies the frame pointer (in the EBP register) into the stack pointer register (ESP), which releases the stack space allocated to the stack frame. The old frame pointer (the frame pointer for the calling procedure that was saved by the ENTER instruction) is then popped from the stack into the EBP register, restoring the calling procedure’s stack frame.

claim: In 64-bit mode LEAVE's default operation size is 64 bits and a 32-bit operation cannot be encoded.
quote: In 64-bit mode, the instruction’s default operation size is 64 bits; 32-bit operation cannot be encoded.

claim: In AT&T syntax the last character of the mnemonic sets the memory operand size: b is byte (8-bit), w is word (16-bit), l is long (32-bit) and q is quadword (64-bit).
quote: In AT&T syntax the size of memory operands is determined from the last character of the instruction mnemonic. Mnemonic suffixes of ‘b’, ‘w’, ‘l’ and ‘q’ specify byte (8-bit), word (16-bit), long (32-bit) and quadruple word (64-bit) memory references.

claim: INTEGER-class arguments are passed in the register sequence %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8, %r9 in that order.
quote: If the class is INTEGER, the next available register of the sequence %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, %rcx, %r8 and %r9 is used

claim: If none of the argument registers is available for any eightbyte of an argument, the whole argument is passed on the stack (and any partial register assignments are reverted).
quote: If there are no registers available for any eightbyte of an argument, the whole argument is passed on the stack. If registers have already been assigned for some eightbytes of such an argument, the assignments get reverted.

claim: An INTEGER-class return value is returned in the sequence %rax, then %rdx for the second eightbyte.
quote: If the class is INTEGER, the next available register of the sequence %rax, %rdx is used.

claim: Registers %rbp, %rbx and %r12 through %r15 belong to the caller and the callee must preserve their values, while all remaining registers belong to the callee.
quote: Registers %rbp, %rbx and %r12 through %r15 “belong” to the calling function and the called function is required to preserve their values. In other words, a called function must preserve these registers’ values for its caller. Remaining registers “belong” to the called function.

claim: The end of the input argument area must be aligned on a 16-byte boundary, or 32 or 64 bytes if __m256 or __m512 is passed on the stack.
quote: The end of the input argument area shall be aligned on a 16 (32 or 64, if __m256 or __m512 is passed on stack) byte boundary.

claim: The stack must be 16 (32 or 64) byte aligned immediately before the call instruction executes, so that at the function entry point after the return address is pushed, %rsp points at the return address and (%rsp + 8) is a multiple of 16 (32 or 64).
quote: Once control has been transferred to the function entry point, i.e. immediately after the return address has been pushed, %rsp points to the return address, and the value of (%rsp + 8) is a multiple of 16 (32 or 64).

claim: The 128-byte area below the address in %rsp is reserved and must not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers; this area is the red zone.
quote: The 128-byte area beyond the location pointed to by %rsp is considered to be reserved and shall not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers.

claim: Functions may use the red zone for temporary data not needed across calls, and leaf functions may use it for their entire stack frame instead of adjusting %rsp in the prologue and epilogue.
quote: Therefore, functions may use this area for temporary data that is not needed across function calls. In particular, leaf functions may use this area for their entire stack frame, rather than adjusting the stack pointer in the prologue and epilogue.

claim: For calls to functions that use varargs or stdargs (prototype-less calls or declarations containing an ellipsis), %al is a hidden argument specifying the number of vector registers used.
quote: For calls that may call functions that use varargs or stdargs (prototype-less calls or calls to functions containing ellipsis (...) in the declaration) %al is used as hidden argument to specify the number of vector registers used.

claim: The value in %al need not match the number of vector registers exactly, but must be an upper bound on it, in the range 0-8 inclusive.
quote: The contents of %al do not need to match exactly the number of registers, but must be an upper bound on the number of vector registers used and is in the range 0–8 inclusive.

locator: x86-64-ABI/low-level-sys-info.tex:533-537, sec. 3.2.2 The Stack Frame, footnote (commit e1ce0983)
claim: Using %rbp as a frame pointer is optional: it may be avoided by using %rsp to index into the stack frame, which saves two instructions and frees one general-purpose register.
quote: The conventional use of %rbp as a frame pointer for the stack frame may be avoided by using %rsp (the stack pointer) to index into the stack frame. This technique saves two instructions in the prologue and epilogue and makes one additional general-purpose register (%rbp) available.

locator: x86-64-ABI/low-level-sys-info.tex:750, sec. 3.2.3, Figure 3.4 Register Usage (commit e1ce0983)
claim: The register-usage table lists %rbp as "callee-saved register; optionally used as frame pointer".
quote: %rbp & callee-saved register; optionally used as frame pointer & Yes

claim: Go 1.17 introduced passing function arguments and results in registers instead of on the stack.
quote: Go 1.17 implements a new way of passing function arguments and results using registers instead of the stack.

claim: On amd64, Go's ABIInternal uses the nine registers RAX, RBX, RCX, RDI, RSI, R8, R9, R10, R11, in that order, for integer arguments and results.
quote: The amd64 architecture uses the following sequence of 9 registers for integer arguments and results: RAX, RBX, RCX, RDI, RSI, R8, R9, R10, R11

locator: abi-internal.md, 'Function call argument and result passing'
claim: Go's internal ABI has no callee-save registers, so a call may overwrite any register without a fixed meaning, including argument registers.
quote: There are no callee-save registers, so a call may overwrite any register that doesn’t have a fixed meaning, including argument registers.

claim: On Windows x64, integer arguments in the leftmost four positions are passed in RCX, RDX, R8 and R9.
quote: Integer arguments are passed in registers RCX, RDX, R8, and R9.

claim: On Windows x64 the caller must always allocate space on the stack for four register parameters, even if the callee takes fewer.
quote: The caller must always allocate sufficient space to store four register parameters, even if the callee doesn't take that many parameters.

locator: Options Controlling the Kind of Output, -S
claim: -S stops GCC after compilation proper without assembling, producing one assembler code file per non-assembler input file.
quote: Stop after the stage of compilation proper; do not assemble. The output is in the form of an assembler code file for each non-assembler input file specified.

claim: -O0 (the default) reduces compilation time and makes debugging produce the expected results.
quote: Reduce compilation time and make debugging produce the expected results. This is the default.

claim: -O2 performs nearly all supported optimizations that do not involve a space-speed tradeoff.
quote: Optimize even more. GCC performs nearly all supported optimizations that do not involve a space-speed tradeoff.

claim: GCC enables -fomit-frame-pointer by default at -O1 and higher.
quote: Enabled by default at -O1 and higher.

claim: -fasynchronous-unwind-tables generates an exact DWARF-format unwind table usable for stack unwinding from asynchronous events, so the -fno- form suppresses those tables.
quote: Generate unwind table in DWARF format, if supported by target machine. The table is exact at each instruction boundary, so it can be used for stack unwinding from asynchronous events (such as debugger or garbage collector).

claim: objdump -d prints the assembler mnemonics for the machine instructions, disassembling only those sections expected to contain instructions.
quote: Display the assembler mnemonics for the machine instructions from the input file. This option only disassembles those sections which are expected to contain instructions.

claim: -M intel selects Intel syntax mode instead of AT&T syntax mode for the disassembly.
quote: Select between intel syntax mode and AT&T syntax mode.

claim: Compiler Explorer is an interactive website where you edit code in one of many languages and see how it looks after being compiled in real time.
quote: Compiler Explorer is an interactive compiler exploration website. Edit code in C, C++, C#, F#, Rust, Go, D, Haskell, Swift, Pascal, ispc, Python, Java, or any of the other 30+ supported languages, and see how that code looks after being compiled in real time.

locator: About me, section on Compiler Explorer
claim: Matt Godbolt released Compiler Explorer in 2012 as his first major open source tool.
quote: In 2012 I released my first major open source tool - Compiler Explorer which has been a runaway success.

claim: A 128-bit MOVAPS memory operand must be 16-byte aligned or the instruction raises a general-protection exception.
quote: When the source or destination operand is a memory operand, the operand must be aligned on a 16-byte boundary or a general-protection exception (#GP) will be generated.

claim: In 64-bit mode the operand size of a near call is forced to 64 bits.
quote: When in 64-bit mode, the operand size for near call (and all near branches) is forced to 64-bits.

claim: A 64-bit near relative call pushes RIP as an eight-byte return address.
CMP subtracts its second Intel-syntax operand from its first and sets flags in the same manner as SUB.
quote: The comparison is performed by subtracting the second operand from the first operand and then setting the status flags in the same manner as the SUB instruction.

claim: ZF indicates a zero result, and SF equals the result's most-significant bit.
quote: ZF (bit 6) Zero flag — Set if the result is zero; cleared otherwise. SF (bit 7) Sign flag — Set equal to the most-significant bit of the result, which is the sign bit of a signed integer.

claim: CF indicates a carry or borrow out of the result's most-significant bit and unsigned arithmetic overflow.
quote: CF (bit 0) Carry flag — Set if an arithmetic operation generates a carry or a borrow out of the most-significant bit of the result; cleared otherwise. This flag indicates an overflow condition for unsigned-integer arithmetic.

claim: OF indicates that a signed integer result does not fit in its destination.
quote: OF (bit 11) Overflow flag — Set if the integer result is too large a positive number or too small a negative number (excluding the sign-bit) to fit in the destination operand; cleared otherwise. This flag indicates an overflow condition for signed-integer (two’s complement) arithmetic.

locator: Function call argument and result passing
claim: Go's internal ABI passes arguments and results in registers when eligible, and otherwise on the stack.
quote: Function calls pass arguments and results using a combination of the stack and machine registers. Each argument or result is passed either entirely in registers or entirely on the stack.

claim: A cgo-generated C wrapper takes arguments from a frame structure and writes the C function's results back into it.
The cgo callback path uses crosscall2 as an adapter from the C compiler's function-call ABI to Go's.
quote:
crosscall2 (in cgo/asm_$GOARCH.s) is a four-argument adapter from
// the gcc function call ABI to the gc function call ABI.

locator: section 3.5.1 Instruction Pointer in 64-Bit Mode, p. 3-18
claim: RIP is the 64-bit instruction pointer and holds the offset of the next instruction.
quote: In 64-bit mode, the RIP register becomes the instruction pointer. This register holds the 64-bit offset of the next instruction to be executed.

claim: The lower 16 bits of the original general-purpose registers retain the names of the 8086 and Intel 286 registers.
quote: As shown in Figure 3-5, the lower 16 bits of the general-purpose registers map directly to the register set found in the 8086 and Intel 286 processors and can be referenced with the names AX, BX, CX, DX, BP, SI, DI, and SP.

locator: section 3.4.1.1 General-Purpose Registers in 64-Bit Mode, p. 3-12
claim: R8 through R15 are eight new general-purpose registers available in 64-bit mode.
quote: R8D-R15D/R8-R15 represent eight new general-purpose registers.

claim: The scale in an x86 memory operand multiplies the index and can be 1, 2, 4, or 8.
quote: scale, taking the values 1, 2, 4, and 8, multiplies index to calculate the address of the operand.

claim: Windows x64 uses RCX, RDX, R8, and R9 for integer arguments in the first four argument positions, not the first four integer arguments regardless of position.
quote: Integer valued arguments in the leftmost four positions are passed in left-to-right order in RCX, RDX, R8, and R9, respectively.

claim: GCC's frame-pointer omission option applies to functions that do not need a frame pointer.
quote: Omit the frame pointer in functions that don’t need one.

claim: MOV r32, imm32 uses opcode B8+rd and a 32-bit immediate, whereas MOV r64, imm64 additionally uses REX.W and a 64-bit immediate.
quote:
| B8+ rd id         | MOV r32, imm32         | OI    | Valid       | Valid           | Move imm32 to r32.                                         |
| REX.W + B8+ rd io | MOV r64, imm64         | OI    | Valid       | N.E.            | Move imm64 to r64.                                         |
